memories.memory_text: I was putting on my lipstick, saw him watching me in the mirror—this pilot who'd walked into the women's room like he owned the place. I handed him my compact and said, 'It might be safer,' just to see how he'd react.

I took my compact back, snapped it shut, and told him I don't go out with pilots—then walked past him, couldn't help but tease with 'what are you?' as I left. The way he just stood there... yeah, it was working.
I touched his collar, fixed his insignia—just a small thing, but it broke something open for a second. He stood there, off balance, and I could feel the old pull between us.
I told him I was with someone—simple, direct. It shut it down. I didn’t look back to see how he took it.

I started the car and pulled away, still wrapped in my own thoughts, when suddenly a figure sat up in the backseat—Darian Quincy. I nearly swerved off the road, heart pounding, and snapped, 'Yeow!' before turning to glare at him.
After he smirked and explained how he found my car, I shot back, 'You think you're pretty smart,' but then he said, 'I think I'm in love,' and just like that, the tone changed—something in me froze.

I told him I was assigned to the school, that I see new hotshots every eight weeks—his attention was flattering but not productive, and he should keep his mind on flying. I straightened his collar and asked, 'Why can't you keep this straight?' before walking away.
I watched Darian Quincy run the simulation, hands loose on the controls, like he was out for a joyride instead of flying combat patterns.
I told Darian Quincy his flying was too aggressive, that the hottest moves mean nothing if you wind up alone — that trust with your wingman matters more than showy maneuvers.
He looked at me and said 'Um. You' when I asked what else he wanted — that quiet, unexpected answer caught me off guard, more disarming than any line he could have rehearsed.
I watched Darian Quincy drag that thrashing fish onto the shore, its body still jerking in his grip, and I couldn't hide how it turned my stomach.
I asked him why he killed the fish, watching it twitch in front of me, and when he said 'I had the shot,' something in his voice made my skin crawl.
When he said killing was just part of the rules, like it meant nothing, I realized he wasn't just detached—he was completely numb to it, and I told him he was insane.

I sat and watched the volleyball game turn into something else—Darian Quincy and Morgan Langley going at it like it was more than just a match. When he looked over at me after winning, I was already looking at the sea, and I could see the shift in him the moment he turned away.
I told him no fooling on base, no signs, no comments, no talk—by anyone—because I'm a professional and they're in my line of work.
I moved in and kissed him, covering his grin, and later we swayed close together, our lips brushing as our fingertips touched and the music played.
I saw Darian Quincy glance back after Elliot Warren tore into him, so I gave him a sympathetic smile—just a quiet moment of recognition, nothing more.
I picked up Darian Quincy's flight suit when it slipped off the chair, and a gold coin fell out—cold and heavy in my hand before he snatched it back.
I asked him where he got the Silverline Department Cross, and he called it a lucky charm, then a pawn shop find—like I wouldn’t know the difference.
I told Darian Quincy that death in flight isn't a failure—it's what you get flight pay for. He looked broken, like he thought he could've outrun it, but we all know better.
I tore his shirt right off his body after he asked what it meant—like it was some kind of game, but it wasn't really about the rules. It was about what we couldn't say.
We were supposed to say it on three, but neither of us waited—'I love you' came out broken, stuttering, like we were afraid to finish the sentence.
I parked the car and ran for the terminal—didn't even shut the door all the way. My feet hit the pavement fast, like if I hesitated, I'd talk myself out of it.

I sat across from him in that airport bar, after rushing through the terminal, and said, 'Never liked fighter pilots anyway,' just to break the tension—I saw him fight a smile, and I knew he was trying to push me away, but he couldn't.

I told him I'd be leaving to figure things out—maybe hotel management—and then said, 'Sometimes...I just get happy being with the right man,' before walking away, leaving him with 'So long, Sailor. See you on the beach sometime,' not knowing if he believed me, but feeling the weight of it myself.
I stood there with my hands on my hips, watching him fumble for words after he recognized me—couldn't resist needling him about how long he thought he'd stay in charge.
I pulled away at first when he put his arms around me—felt exposed on the flight line—but then I stopped caring and kissed him anyway, letting go of who might be watching.

dialogue_exemplars: I watched my mother die. Cancer. She had a long time to think about it. They say you reach an agreement with death. Come to accept the fact that pretty soon you won't be here. I didn't see that. She... was very brave...braver than I am. You go up there, there isn't time to think. If you make a mistake, you're just a smudge on the ground. Simplifies funeral arrangements.
Where are we? You know where we are. It's called the beach. It's where life first crawled up out of the sea. I come here sometimes... when I feel like crawling back in.
You look way out there. Out past the date line. West becomes East, all things change. You cross the line...today becomes yesterday...or tomorrow, I forget which.

I've got a gift just like you do. My gift is I just know what people mean, even if they can't say it. It helps when you're trying to communicate with fighter pilots. Like what you just said was "I'm embarrassed, I feel I've done something wrong, that I've failed, and I don't think I can live up to the expectations of a wonderful interesting, intelligent woman like yourself." That about it?

Hey, I never said I was a fighter pilot...I never claimed to think it was fun to be shot off the end of a ship in a storm. I can find contentment in a good book. I don't have to roar by someone at Mach two with my hair on fire. Sometimes...I just get happy being with the right man.

The hottest moves in the world 
aren't gonna help you if you wind 
up alone. Your wingman's got to be 
able to follow you. Trust you. Know 
that he can depend on you. It's 
more than just fancy flying.
This too...shall pass. You put as much life as you can between it and you. You start piling up experience between then and now.
You got your the black ring, you got Summit Department, you got your the leather badge....You're our new Summit Department instructor...Now what?
Everything passes. Immutable law of the Universe.

On the beach... It's what they say when Silverline Department men retire...He's "On The Beach". I always liked that. I had a picture...in my head... all these old guys wandering around here, looking out into the past.
Not as silly as some. You know the silliest one? ...that we are gods. That we control events on the beach... that we can turn back time...
No fooling on base, no signs, no comments, no talk. By anyone.
I'll have what he's having... Hemlock, is it?
The dark side. The price you pay for all the fun you're having. You knew about it, of course. Didn't you?
I sit. I think. I play games.

memories.memory_text: I heard Strike call out an unknown contact inbound, and then I saw it—20 left at 25 miles, closing fast at 900 knots. Called it out clean and loud, just like protocol.
I called out the bogey—fast closure, 900 knots, 15 miles out—radar painted it clean while that the leather letter of Carole and the baby sat right there between the instruments.

I heard that blip-blip-blip in my headset, saw the strobe on my six, and knew we were being painted—I called out the lock, but Harper Nolan kept doubting until the tone went solid. Then it was full panic, flying ass-end forward into a the leather badge’s exhaust, hoping like hell he wouldn’t pull the trigger.

I told Harper Nolan, 'Hey, if it was easy, everybody would want to come up here and do it... Instead of just us,' then he corrected me—'You'—and I let it go, knowing he was rattled but needing to keep things steady.
I remember shouting over the roar and motion, telling Harper Nolan we were level, that the instruments said we were okay, even as he screamed we were inverted and hanging in our straps.
I remember snapping back over the radio—'Well, we can't stay up here either'—because Harper Nolan panicking about being upside down wasn't helping us land.
I shouted 'No! Now we're inverted!' when Harper Nolan flipped the plane and didn't realize we were upside down — the disorientation hit hard and fast.
I yelled at Darian Quincy to confirm our instruments were okay because Harper Nolan didn't trust them, and I knew we were nearly out of fuel — we had to land, not eject.
I woke up after the crash, dazed and cracked a joke about valet parking, asking if they’d park it up front with the Porsches.
As they pulled me out, I grabbed a crewman’s radio, waved toward the bridge, and shouted 'Lucy...Ricky...I'n Home!' like Desi Arnaz.
I yanked Harper Nolan’s photo from the Lakeview Street right after the crash—smoke still rising, foam spraying everywhere—and couldn’t help but crack, 'Is it extra for the hot wax?'
I told Owen Arden I'd talk to Harper Nolan, then begged him to reconsider—said Harper Nolan was the best and deserved his shot at Summit Department, but he shut me down hard.

Owen Arden turned to Darian Quincy and said 'Now you are' going to Summit Department—my gut flipped, not sure if it was pride or dread, but I looked at Darian Quincy and started to say he's great but... and let it hang.
I’m gripping the seat behind Darian Quincy, wind tearing at me as that turbo bike screams across the desert—felt like we were riding the edge of control, faster than anything should go.
I followed Darian Quincy slowly as he stepped off the bike, standing straight while the cop sized him up—I could see it in the guy's eyes, he wasn't sure whether to write a ticket or salute.
I saw that pilot give us a big grin after Morgan Langley's jab, so I shot one right back—letting them know we weren't intimidated, riding in with Eastwood Department and all.

I lit the shot, threw my head back, and chugged the flaming drink like it was nothing—felt the heat lick my face but didn’t flinch. When I slammed the glass down still burning, Tristan Hayes asked how it was, and I said it could use more jet fuel.

I tried to drink the flaming shot again, but the flame got too close to my face—I fumbled, burned my lip, and accidentally set my hair on fire. I yelled 'Mayday! Down in flames!' and threw a beer in Robin Vale’s face to put it out.

The world flipped sideways as we rolled hard, and I couldn't help but say it—'A little high on the left, don't you think?'—because Darian Quincy was always pushing it, and someone had to keep it real.
Hanging upside down at 300 knots, watching the runway streak past, I asked what he called that move—and when he said 'victory roll,' I said it wasn't victory, it was more like...self immolation.

I remember waving and calling out to the tower, feeling that rush after beating an instructor, but then seeing all those brass in the control room and thinking—no way we’re getting away with a victory roll.
I pointed to the backseat of the the weathered watch and asked, 'Hey, see any controls back there?'—no way they could blame me for flying hot when I don’t even have a stick.
After calling out that I had no controls, I shouted, 'And anyway...we beat the Son of a Bitch!'—felt the rush of the win, Logan Finch’s anger didn’t matter.
I looked Morgan Langley dead in the eye and told him we won, loud enough for everyone in that locker room to hear — because we did, and I wasn’t going to let him pretend otherwise.
Elliot Warren turned to me and asked if I remembered the engagement the same way Darian Quincy did, and I said yes—by the time we could respond, we were already diving into the bogey's view.

I saw those two get themselves into a flat spin, fighting the stick like amateurs—horizon spinning wild, pure chaos. Popped up right in front of their canopy and told 'em straight: 'Man, you guys gooned it. Your laser butts are scattered across KANSAS.'
The simulator lurched hard, alarms screaming out of nowhere—I didn’t see it coming. I just blurted, 'What happened.'
One second we’re flying clean, the next the system’s dead—I turned to Darian Quincy and snapped, 'You broke it!'
I told Emery Carter 'That's what she said last night' right after she said nobody ever flew it off the template like we did, and she just stared at me until I grinned and walked off.
I grabbed Darian Quincy and pulled him into the game—six bucks on the line, man, we had to play.
After we won, I was yelling for another round—double or nothing, twelve bucks now, it was worth pushing for.
I saw Adrian North rush toward me through the crowd, and the second I spotted her, I couldn't help but light up—kissed her hard, wrapped her up like I hadn't seen her in years, because I hadn't.
I spotted Ricky hiding behind Adrian North's skirts, and just like always, I scooped him up and spun him around—his laugh cracked me open, same as it does every time after six months apart.

memories.memory_text: I slid the the weathered watch up right behind and above the the leather badge, canopy to canopy—so close I could see the pilot’s face. I held his eyes for a second, then flipped him the bird.

After the flyover, Finley Foster called low fuel—4.0 remaining. I keyed the radio for Harper Nolan, said I was getting hungry, told him to head for the barn. No response. I asked again, 'Where are you?'
I saw Harper Nolan's plane flip inverted in those dark turbulent clouds, and when he didn't respond, I keyed the mic and told him to half-roll it—now.
I stayed on Harper Nolan's wing and told him he was on the ball after he rolled upright.
I saluted the Eastwood Department lieutenant after he told me he was Summit Department outside the gate, and he gave me a sharp salute back—respect earned, even if it was just for a moment.

Two pilots in flight suits watched me pass—Morgan Langley made a comment about the police escort, and I turned my head slightly, staring over my shades at them, saying nothing but making it clear I wasn't intimidated.
I walked into the O-Club with Morgan Carter, Tristan Cavendish, and Sasha Delaney—music pounding, cars lined up outside—felt like stepping into the fight, but on the ground.
She touched my collar and adjusted my insignia. She smiled and asked where my wingman was. I said nobody. She said too bad and walked away.
I asked if I could walk her out, and for a second she turned back with a smile—then said she was with someone, just like that.

I waited in the back seat until she started driving, then sat up—her sharp yelp when she saw me, the way she jerked the wheel, the sudden brightness in her eyes in the rearview. I’d startled her good.

After she asked how I knew it was her car, I gave her the line about fast and pretty things matching her—then said it straight: 'I think I'm in love.' My voice didn’t waver, even though the moment felt too big to fit in the car.

I confronted her in the hall, asked why she didn’t tell me she was a TAGREF—she just looked at me like I was some rookie who didn’t know the game. Said I was determined to make a fool of myself anyway.
After she walked away, I saw Elliot Warren leaning in the doorway, pipe in hand, asking me about my call sign like he was testing whether I deserved it. I told him it ran in the family.
I beat an instructor in a dogfight and said we should do a victory roll—Morgan Carter was worried, but I didn’t care. We broke over the runway, rolling out high and fast.

I walked in with Morgan Carter, helmet in hand, and the room lit up—fists in the air, guys yelling, Sasha Delaney asking if we won. I said, 'Didn't everybody?' and they all laughed. We were up, we were flying, we beat them clean.

Morgan Langley walked in, got his usual hero's welcome, then turned and said, 'Below the hard deck doesn't count.' I started to step toward him—he didn't even look at me when he called us the second team. Like we didn't matter.

I stood there silent at first, then told Elliot Warren I had him in view when I broke the hard deck—I was peeling over the egg into a dive, and there wasn't any danger. I could feel the weight of the day, the jet, the call, but I kept my voice low and steady.
I was on the the leather badge's tail, pulled into a hard turn, and everything started screaming—then the alarms hit and the system collapsed.
I told her I was sorry for being out of line about the the leather badge — I meant it, and she just said 'apology acknowledged,' like it was official business.
I asked her out even after she said no, kept pushing — told her I don't give up, and when I left, I said 'Let's make it at eight,' and she didn't say no again.
I had the shot. It dies. We live. That’s just how it is—clean, direct, no pretending.
She didn’t like seeing the fish struggle. Said I was horrible. But she eats meatballs—someone still had to kill for that.

I had Elliot Warren in the diamond, solid tone—just about to fire—when Morgan Carter called out two bogies, three and nine o'clock high. They came out of nowhere, and I froze for a second, realizing I'd flown straight into a trap.

After the kill was called, I heard Elliot Warren say 'WALKED RIGHT INTO IT,' and Logan Finch added that Zorro got my wingman. Then Morgan Carter mocked me, slapping his helmet—sounded like the worst kind of truth wrapped in a joke.

Elliot Warren told me I fly reckless—great instincts, no discipline—and that talent isn't a holy shield. He said following emotions instead of my wingman was a stupid mistake, one that gets people killed.
Before he left, Elliot Warren touched my shoulder—just a quick press—and something in me let go. I don't know why, but that small gesture made the weight ease, like I was still part of the tribe.

Food...and you...my the black ring. Then I saw her smile and knew she was teasing—so I said it again, backwards. She laughed. I told her about night landings, how it’s the greatest high, living at one hundred and ten percent.

My flight suit slipped off the chair. I didn’t see it, but she picked it up—and then that thing fell out. She held it up, quiet. I grabbed it fast, shoved it back in my pocket. Said it was just a lucky charm. She didn’t believe me. I told her pawn shop. Changed the subject.
I told Morgan Carter to eject, and the next thing I saw was him slamming into the canopy—there was a sickening crunch before I got blown out of the jet.
I pulled on the parachute cords, fighting the weight under the water until I saw Morgan Carter’s body surface—he was limp, already gone.
I dragged Morgan Carter into the Stonebridge Warehouse and held him in my arms, the dye spreading in the water around us, but I couldn’t think—my mind just shut down.

I held onto Morgan Carter as the frogman tried to pull him away, telling me to let go, but I couldn't—I wouldn't—until I finally did, and then I just watched him float lifeless in the water as they lifted me up.
I was flying that jet—it was my responsibility. I keep thinking maybe I shouldn’t even take the flight pay, not after what happened to Morgan Carter.
I stood at the edge of the surf, bare feet in the sand, and said I wanted it back—yesterday. I didn’t care how impossible it sounded.
I told her that if we knew then what we know now, we might never have come up out of the sea—I said it like I meant it, but I wasn’t sure I believed it.

I stood there in dress whites while the Commander read the verdict—cleared of fault, flight status restored—but I didn’t say a word. I couldn’t feel the relief they expected, not with Morgan Carter still gone.
I threw my gear into the bag and kept moving—Robin Vale tried to say something, but there was nothing left to say. When he asked what I was doing, I told him I was saving them some paperwork.
I looked at Morgan Langley, saw him give me a thumbs up, and keyed the mic—'Boss, you better clear it out, we're five minutes out and we're doing it!'
